sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why did the British pressurise Indian farmers to cultivate indigo?
questions.answer: (1) Gradually they wanted to conquer the vast territory of India for which they needed a lot of money. Indigo was sent to England and used as a dyeing agent for cloth produced in British towns. (2) Indians were forced to produce indigo and sell it on the conditions dictated by the Britishers. Indigo was grown under a different system where all farmers were compelled to grow it on 3/20th part of their land.

questions.q: Mention any two reforms brought by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in the field of education.
questions.answer: (1) The Arya Samaj founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in 1875 undertook the task of reforming Hindu religion in North India. The use of Hindi language in which he wrote and preached made his ideas accessible to the people of Northern India. (2) Some of Swami Dayanand’s followers later started a network of schools and colleges called D.A.V. (Dayanand Anglo Vedic) in the country to impart education on western lines without compromising on the Vedic teachings. They encouraged teaching of English and modern science along with Sanskrit and Vedic education.

questions.q: Explain the number of judges, including the Chief Justice, in the Supreme Court of India.
questions.answer: (1) As provided in the Constitution, the Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief Justice and other Judges whose number is prescribed by the Parliament from time to time. The Chief Justice and other Judges are appointed by the President. (2) In 1950 there was a Chief Justice and 7 judges; the number has been increased with need — the textbook gives a Chief Justice and 30 judges.

questions.q: How do political parties help in running democratic processes?
questions.answer: (1) Political parties actually help the institutions and processes of a government democratic. They enable people to participate in elections and other processes of governance, educate them and facilitate them to make policy choices. (2) They place objectives and programmes before the voters through their manifestos; those securing the majority in elections form the government and enact and implement the policies; they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion.

questions.q: What is meant by criminalisation of politics? How can it be checked?
questions.answer: (1) There have been allegations that there are some elements in politics who do not have faith in democratic values and practices. Criminalization of politics is the very negation of democratic values. (2) We, as awakened citizens and as voters of the largest democracy in the world, can also contribute by discouraging such persons who have a criminal background, from contesting elections.

questions.q: 'Peace and security are inseparable.' Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Peace cannot exist where people live under threat, and security is meaningless without harmony. (2) Conflict not only generates threat and fear, but also hampers economic, social, or political advancement. It is a condition where individuals, institutions, regions, nations and the world move ahead without any threat.

questions.q: 'India has a unique geographical location.' Support the statement.
questions.answer: (1) Teacher: India lies entirely in the northern hemisphere, and eastern hemisphere. The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′North) passes through the centre of the country. India is located between 8°4’ North and 37°6’ North lalitudes and 68°7’ East and 97°25’ longitudes. (2) It is surrounded by sea on three sides and lies at the centre of the Indian Ocean, commanding sea routes between Europe/Africa and East Asia, which helps trade. (3) The Himalayas form a natural barrier in the north, while passes link it with neighbours for trade and cultural exchange.

questions.q: Analyse any three characteristics of road transport in India.
questions.answer: (1) Roads provide door to door service by means of a rickshaw, car, bicycle, bus, scooter or a truck. It is through roads that we reach railway stations, airports and seaports. (2) It is the cheapest and the most convenient mode of transportation for a few people and relatively smaller amount of goods over shorter distances. (3) Roads connect rural areas to the urban areas and can be constructed in all types of terrains like hills, deserts, mountain and plateaus.

or.q: Analyse any three characteristics of rail transport in India.
or.answer: (1) This is the cheapest transport by which thousands of people can travel together from one corner of the country to another for the purpose of ducation, business, siteseeing, pilgrimage or visiting friends or relatives. One can have comfortable night journey as it has berths and washrooms in sleeper coaches. Railways are generally used for long distances. (2) It carries country’s largest amount of bulky goods like coal, cement, food grains, fertilizer, petroleum, automobiles etc. from mines to industries and from industries to the areas of consumption. (3) It is the largest network in Asia (over 64,000 km), the largest government undertaking, divided into 16 zones, with modern facilities like e-tickets and electric locomotives.

questions.q: Suggest any three corrective measures for universal literacy (education for all).
questions.answer: (1) As a follow up of the National Policy on Education 1986 , a National Literacy Mission was set up in 1988 to plan and implement programmes for the removal of illiteracy under the platform, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. passed Right to Education Act through which education has become a fundamental right of all children in the age group of 6-14 years. (2) Adult literacy through the National Literacy Mission and Saakshar Bharat (functional literacy for those above 15). (3) Special attention to girls and disadvantaged groups — scholarships, mid-day meals, more schools in remote areas.

questions.q: Why are peace and security essential for the progress of individuals, nations and the world? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) No development activity is possible if there is disturbance, violence or war. (2) Peace and security is an essential condition for democracy and development. (3) Conflict not only generates threat and fear, but also hampers economic, social, or political advancement. It is through development that nations can ensure social and economic progress for the people and improve their quality of life.

questions.q: On the given outline map of India, mark and label: (A) Shimla, a tourist place in the Middle Himalaya (B) Western Ghats (C) River Krishna (D) Gir Range.
questions.answer: (A) Shimla — in Himachal Pradesh, about 31°N, 77°E, in the Lesser Himalaya (Himachal). (B) Western Ghats — a continuous line along the west coast from the Tapi (Maharashtra/Gujarat border) south to Kanyakumari. (C) Krishna — rises in the Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar, flows east through Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh to the Bay of Bengal. (D) Gir Range — in the Kathiawar (Saurashtra) peninsula of Gujarat.

questions.q: Explain any six legislative powers of the President.
questions.answer: (1) (b) Legislative Powers: The President is an integral part of the Parliament and in this capacity he/she enjoys many legislative powers. (2) He/She summons and prorogues the sessions of Parliament and can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Council of Ministers. He/She is elected by an electoral college which consists of the members of both Houses of the Parliament. (3) Dissolves the Lok Sabha- When the President dissolves the Lok Sabha, it means that the House ceases to exist till it is reconstituted after the next elections. And that is not a simple advice, but is binding. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. (4) The President addresses the Parliament every year at the commencement of the first session and after each general election to the Lok Sabha. (5) Without his/her assent no bill can become a law or an Act. Once the bill is passed by both the Houses, it is sent to the President for his/ her assent and with his/her assent it becomes a law or an act. If the Rajya Sabha along with its recommendations (if any) does not return it to Lok Sabha within 14 days, the bill is deemed to have been passed by both the Houses. (6) Calls a joint sitting to resolve deadlocks, issues ordinances when Parliament is not in session, and nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.

or.q: Explain the meaning of the Electoral College in the Indian Presidential election. What qualifications are required for a person to be elected President of India?
or.answer: (1) He/She is elected according to the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferrable vote, and the voting is by secret ballot. He/She is indirectly elected by an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both the Houses of the Parliament and the State Legislative Assemblies. (2) (vi) (i) a citizen of India (ii) of at least 25 years of age (iii) not hold an office (3) (ii) must have been at least a Judge of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession for at least five years; or (ii) (a) be a citizen of India (b) have completed the age of 35 years (c) be qualified for being elected as a Member of Lok Sabha (d) not hold any office of profit (4) (iii) be qualified for being elected as a member of the House of the People (Lok Sabha); and (5) (iv) not hold any office of profit under the government of India, any State government or under any local authority or any other authority of the said government. There is a provision for the re-election of a person who is holding or who has held the office as President. His/Her term of office is for five years, though he/she can be removed even before through impeachment.
